the kettle remembers how to become a voice.  
The cat, if there is one,  
is a soft punctuation mark  
at the end of the room.  
Somewhere a tree is making decisions  
with its hundred thousand leaves,  
and no one calls this dramatic.

Perhaps this is enough of a creed:  
to believe in the quiet labor of things,  
the unseen tenderness  
with which the dark makes room for dawn,  
the way the old griefs  
do not vanish but thin out,  
becoming like weather in another county—  
still real, but no longer standing in the doorway.

So let the hour be ordinary.  
Let the bread rise.  
Let the ash cool.  
Let the unremarkable light  
rest on the sink, the handle, the wall,  
and be received  
as a hand resting lightly on the shoulder.

We are here  
for the brief assembly of stillness,  
for the blade of grass lifting its face,  
for the cracked bowl holding peaches,  
for the names we whisper  
to things that cannot answer  
except by remaining.

And this, too, is a kind of answer:  
the room, breathing.  
The page, unafraid.  
The world, in its small persistent way,  
offering itself again.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
A little farther on,  
the evening begins to unfasten its sleeves.  
The lemon on the counter  
keeps the shape of a small sun  
that has agreed not to burn.

There is a softness  
to the way the house forgets itself:  
the stair that no longer insists,  
the coat by the door  
holding the outline of departure,  
the keyring’s modest music  
when touched by a passing breeze.

I have seen the moon  
through a kitchen window  
and thought:  
even this, even now,  
is only a version of listening.  
Light arriving late.  
Glass taking it in.  
The sink, the faucet, the blue dishcloth  
all participating in a silence  
larger than their names.

What is it to live,  
if not to keep setting down  
our cups, our questions,  
our little accounts of rain?  
To let the day be counted  
not by triumph,  
but by the spoon resting in the saucer,  
by the chair that remains,  
by the neighbor’s lamp  
kindling across the dark  
like a thought that does not need to be finished.

So I will leave this here:  
the unswept threshold,  
the basil in its cracked jar,  
the slow clock making room  
for another minute,  
the bruise on a peach  
deepening into sweetness.

Not a conclusion—  
only a hand opening.  
Only the world,  
still warm from being itself.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
And somewhere beyond the window,  
a train draws its long woolen line  
through the black fields,  
carrying strangers  
into names they have not yet been given.

The last light in the hallway  
leans against the wall  
as if borrowed there,  
as if it might be returned  
with a careful thank you.

A moth folds and unfolds  
its small unreasonable belief  
in the porch bulb.  
The night, for all its vastness,  
has learned to enter softly—  
not as a thief,  
but as a guest removing its shoes.

I think of all the things  
that ask nothing from us  
except to be noticed once:  
the tin bowl catching starshine,  
the uneaten pear,  
the coat pocket with its lint and receipt,  
the far hill turning gradually  
from green to indigo  
as if remembering another life.

And the heart, too,  
keeps this modest labor:  
to go on opening  
to what it cannot keep.  
To be a room  
in which the lamp is lit  
even after no one returns.

So let the evening continue.  
Let it loosen the hems of the trees.  
Let the river hold the sky  
without explanation.  
Let each small thing remain  
exactly as fragile as it is—  
and therefore radiant.

For this, perhaps, is enough:  
to stand here,  
among the ordinary miracles,  
and feel the quiet  
making a place for us.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
And after that,  
the hour does what hours do:  
it passes without apology.  
The porch light hums.  
A glass on the table  
holds the last of the day’s amber.  
Somewhere a faucet remembers  
its patient grammar of drops.

I have begun to trust  
the small arrivals:  
the bread cooling on the board,  
the shadow of leaves  
moving over the ceiling  
like a language I almost know,  
the brief alignment of wind  
and open window  
that feels, for a second,  
like being understood.

No thunder carries this evening.  
No trumpet parts the dark.  
Only the soft attendance  
of the world  
as it gathers its hems,  
touches each object once,  
and leaves them shining  
with their own unrepeatable weight.

If there is a prayer here,  
it is not for rescue  
but for witness—  
for the hand to rest on the railing,  
for the breath to deepen,  
for the small lamp of the mind  
to remain unashamed  
of its tenderness.

Let the train keep going.  
Let the moth depart or stay.  
Let the pear ripen into sweetness  
no one will name.  
Let the dark be dark,  
and the window a window,  
and the heart, still learning,  
a field where even the faintest thing  
may be allowed to bloom.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
The room keeps its own weather.  
The books, closed, are patient.  
The chair by the lamp  
holds the exact shape of waiting.

Outside, a dog barks once  
and the sound goes on  
long after the animal is still.  
That, too, is a kind of truth:  
that things leave their outline  
in the air.

I think of all the ordinary mercies  
that do not announce themselves—  
the socket that fits the plug,  
the shoe that meets the stepping foot,  
the spoon that finds the bowl  
without ceremony,  
the body remembering  
how to carry its sadness  
without dropping it.

Night, now, has its slow authority.  
It lays a hand over the hill,  
over the alley, over the sleeping car,  
and nothing resists it.  
Even the brightest signs  
seem, for a moment,  
to belong to it.

And still, beneath all this surrender,  
something persists in wanting:  
not grandly, not vainly,  
but as grass wants rain,  
as roots want darkness,  
as the eye wants dawn  
before it knowingly understands  
that it has been waiting.

So let the page remain open.  
Let it be touched  
by whatever arrives:  
the unsaid, the unfinished,  
the rinsed cup, the soft hinge,  
the sentence that begins  
without knowing where it will end.

This is enough, perhaps:  
to be here uncorrected,  
to let the hour pass through us,  
to leave a little warmth  
in the place we sat,  
and call it, quietly,  
a kind of belonging.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
And after that, there is the small, unremarked labor  
of becoming again:  
the kettle’s first breath,  
the hand finding its sleeve,  
the key remembering the lock,  
the window admitting  
a pale and undecided light.

There are mornings  
that do not arrive all at once.  
They enter like a cat  
through a door left ajar—  
careful, disbelieving,  
brushing against the threshold  
as if to ask permission  
from the silence.

I have known such mornings  
to make saints of no one,  
and yet to soften everything.  
The cup, the table,  
the crease in the blanket,  
the half-read page  
with its patient corner turned down—  
all of it briefly absolved  
of having to mean more  
than itself.

What a relief to be ordinary.  
To be made, for once,  
of errands and weather,  
of the lint on cuff and collar,  
of a heartbeat that keeps  
its appointment without applause.  
To walk among the unspectacular  
and find it luminous anyway.

The day will ask  
for its usual offerings:  
a clasp undone,  
a message answered too late,  
a little grief placed back  
on the shelf beside the salt.  
But even then  
there is this other thing—  
the inward tilt toward light,  
the almost-forgotten music  
of being alive  
and not yet finished.

So let the window keep opening  
by its own narrow measure.  
Let the air come in  
with its rumors of rain.  
Let the sparrow on the wire  
write and erase its brief note  
against the blank measure of sky.

We do not need to name  
what saves us.  
It may be nothing more  
than this:  
the world continuing,  
the self continuing,  
the two of them  
meeting again and again  
in the narrow bridge  
of a single hour  
and calling it enough.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
And then, after the naming,  
after the small litany of enough,  
there remains still  
the ordinary mercy  
of things not requiring witness.

A spoon resting in a cup.  
Dust turning gold  
in the beam’s thin chapel.  
The old sweater on its chair  
like a body that has learned  
how to wait without complaint.

Even the ache,  
if you hold it gently,  
can become a lantern.  
Not to banish the dark—  
nothing so grand—  
but to make a circle  
where one may stand  
and not be wholly lost.

There are afternoons  
that arrive with their sleeves rolled up,  
all plain intent,  
and ask only this:  
that you attend.  
That you notice  
how the pear on the sill  
keeps its small republic of scent,  
how the rain at the pane  
keeps writing the same forgiveness  
in a language  
we almost understand.

And if the day should thin  
to something nearly transparent,  
if the heart should go on  
with its patient, uncelebrated work,  
then let that be song enough.  
Let the steps on the stair  
be a kind of refrain.  
Let the turning of the key  
be a prayer  
with no need of belief.

For the world, in all its weather,  
is still making room:  
for the unfinished sentence,  
for the bread breaking warm in the hand,  
for the name we answer to  
when called back softly  
from the far edge of ourselves.

And we, who have mistaken  
survival for a lesser art,  
discover again  
its difficult grace—  
that to remain,  
to continue,  
to rise from the chair  
and open the same window  
to the same uncertain sky  
is its own quiet astonishment.

So the page stays empty  
only in the way fields are empty  
before the seed remembers  
what it was meant to be.  
So the silence is not absence  
but waiting,  
and the waiting  
is a kind of listening,  
and the listening  
is how the light enters.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
Then let the page keep breathing.

Let it hold, without argument,  
the chipped bowl,  
the unremarkable morning,  
the small domestic weather  
of keys and spilled tea,  
the way a window latch  
can sound like the beginning  
of mercy.

Let there be no trumpet for this,  
no ceremony large enough  
to mistake it for salvation:  
only the cat by the door,  
only the kettle learning heat,  
only the shirt on the line  
lifting its sleeves  
as if in benediction.

Because the day is often saved  
not by grandeur,  
but by the minute return  
of what asks nothing  
except to be seen:  
the moth at the lamp,  
the crack in the bowl  
where the glaze has thinned to silver,  
the penciled list  
that says milk, onions, call back,  
as though the soul itself  
could be kept in order  
by a few tender imperatives.

And yes, there are losses  
that remain losses,  
names that never grow warm again,  
rooms that do not forgive us  
for leaving them.  
But even there  
something persists:  
a thread in the sleeve,  
a note in the wood,  
the faint insistence  
of a song remembered wrongly  
and therefore, perhaps,  
more truly.

So let the page be a doorstep.  
Let the evening arrive  
with its ordinary hands.  
Let the first star appear  
like something modest  
trying not to disturb us.

And if no one is watching,  
if no one arrives to applaud  
the simple miracle of continuing,  
still—  
the candle keeps doing  
what candles do.  
Still—  
the dark makes room  
for the small flame.

And that, for now,  
is enough to call it lived.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
The page goes on  
with its quiet weather,  
its patient grammar of staying.

A spoon in the sink  
catches the afternoon  
and turns it once,  
slowly,  
as if remembering a river.

Outside, the leaves  
practice their brief applause  
for nothing in particular.  
A bicycle leans  
against the fence  
with the confidence of a thing  
that has arrived  
without needing witness.

And somewhere  
beyond the window’s frame,  
beyond the dog barking  
at an empty street,  
beyond the hours  
that keep their own counsel,  
the world continues  
its unadorned liturgy:

bread rising in the dark,  
rain finding the gutter,  
a child asleep  
with one hand open  
as though still receiving  
what cannot be held.

We live here,  
in the middle distance  
between ruin and breakfast,  
between the letter unsent  
and the apology spoken late,  
between the ash  
and the match.

Still, the table waits.  
Still, the chair offers  
its plain devotion.  
Still, the smallest lamp  
makes a republic  
of the room.

So let this be counted  
among the mercies:  
not perfection,  
not arrival,  
not a door flung wide  
on some final, shining answer—

only this:  
the cup refilled,  
the breath returning,  
the hand touching warm porcelain  
as if to say  
I am here,  
I am here,  
and the day,  
for all its bruises,  
has not yet closed its eyes.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
A window left unlatched  
lets in a thread of evening,  
thin as a seam of silver.

The kettle remembers heat  
before it has any,  
the sugar in its jar  
keeps its small white silence,  
and the floorboards  
speak in the language of weight  
to whoever crosses  
without hurry.

Night will come  
with its coat unbuttoned,  
with its pockets full  
of unasked-for weather.  
It will set a lantern  
in the pine trees,  
wash each roof in a borrowed blue,  
and ask nothing of the houses  
except that they remain.

And they will remain—  
the cracked frame,  
the chipped mug,  
the coat on the hook  
holding the shape of a body  
that has gone out  
to buy milk,  
to walk,  
to think better thoughts,  
to stand under the sky  
and let the sky  
be larger than the day’s bad news.

There are days  
that arrive like stones.  
There are days  
that open like a bird.  
There are days  
we survive by the smallest grammar:  
by yes, by later, by enough,  
by the bruise-colored grace  
of ordinary things  
continuing.

So if this page must end,  
let it end gently:  
with the pencil set down,  
with the lamp still lit,  
with the room unchanged  
except for the fact  
that someone was here  
and called the world  
by its plain names  
and found, for a moment,  
that it answered.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
The room, of course, will not remember  
the exact arrangement of breath,  
but the dust will have learned  
another way to settle.

A little after midnight  
the house makes its private weather:  
pipes settling, glass cooling,  
the old hinge uttering its single note  
like a bird that has made a life  
out of returning.

Outside, the road keeps going  
without certainty,  
picking up the moon  
in thin reflective pieces,  
carrying them past hedges  
and the dark backs of gardens  
where tomatoes sleep  
on their stems like small red memories.

Somewhere, a train  
draws a bright line through the distance.  
Somewhere else, a dog  
barks at what it cannot see  
and is answered only by the wind,  
which has never had the courtesy  
to explain itself.

Still, there is comfort  
in the unremarkable persistence  
of bowls, thresholds, rafters, rain.  
In the way a towel dries.  
In the way a name fits  
in the mouth of someone who loves you.  
In the way morning, eventually,  
comes carrying its pale receipt  
for the night  
and does not ask  
what was broken, only  
what will be used.

And if the heart is a room,  
let it be this one:  
warm enough for lingering,  
wide enough for sorrow,  
small enough to hold  
a single honest lamp  
against the long dark.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
Then let the lamp’s small weather  
gather itself in the corners,  
let the windows keep  
their unpersuaded dark,  
let the kettle remember  
its own small rising.

Let the chairs remain faithful  
to the idea of waiting.  
Let the book on the sill  
open where it was left open,  
as if something still might be found  
by returning.

There are days when the world  
arrives as a series of hinges,  
each one asking only  
to be less lonely,  
each one making its modest complaint  
against the frame.

And there are mornings  
so ordinary they feel borrowed,  
with milk on the step,  
with a newspaper gone soft in the rain,  
with sparrows quarrelling in the hedge  
as if they had inherited  
the whole uncertain sky.

No miracle is necessary.  
Only this:  
the spoon in the cup,  
the shoe by the door,  
the coat with its sleeves still holding  
the shape of arms,  
the small, uncelebrated mercy  
of being expected somewhere  
by someone  
who has not yet given up.

So let the room continue.  
Let it keep its half-lit theology  
of dust and beam,  
its patient grammar of surfaces,  
its ancient belief  
that what is tended  
may outlast the weather.

And if the night returns,  
as it always does,  
let it find us here—  
not victorious, not repaired,  
only present,  
with the lamp still lit  
and the ordinary world  
leaning gently toward dawn.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
And when the dawn arrives,  
it will not announce itself.  
It will simply loosen  
the blue thread from the dark,  
and touch the sink,  
and gather the corners  
of the tablecloth into mercy.

The day will begin  
with the sound of a door latch,  
with water entering a glass,  
with one terrible, beautiful moment  
of deciding to stay.

The trees will rehearse  
their patient green,  
the street will carry  
its small commerce of names,  
and somewhere a window  
will open like a thought  
finally willing to breathe.

We will go on  
with our hands full of weather,  
with our pockets full of lint and keys,  
with the faint, dependable ache  
of having loved what is temporary.

And still—  
the cup will wait for the spoon,  
the bread will wait for the knife,  
the engine of the hour  
will keep its soft insistence.

This is enough,  
the day says.  
This is enough,  
the light says,  
laying its gold across the floor  
like a hand that has known  
how to forgive.

So let us answer  
with whatever tenderness remains.  
Let us set down the weight  
we were never meant to carry  
from one dawn to the next.  
Let us be, for a little while,  
the quiet proof  
that even the unfinished  
can be enough to hold.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
and after that,  
the small miracles begin again:

the kettle remembering  
its old, faithful song,  
the shoes at the threshold  
patient as unsent letters,  
the chair keeping faith  
with the shape of a body  
that has not yet arrived.

There is holiness, too,  
in the plain inventions of morning:  
the rinsed plate,  
the folded towel,  
the broom leaning near the wall  
like a shepherd of dust.

Look—  
the sparrow has made  
a grammar of crumbs.  
Look—  
the vine has climbed  
the fence without asking  
whether it was allowed.  
Look—  
even the silence  
is working,  
sewing a soft hem  
into the edges of the world.

If sorrow comes,  
let it come in its own weather.  
We will set another chair  
by the window.  
We will pour it tea.  
We will not mistake it  
for an ending.

And if joy comes,  
we will not fasten it down.  
We will let it move through us  
like light through a clean pane,  
like wind through linens,  
like a name spoken gently  
and answered.

For the heart is only ever  
a borrowed room,  
and all we can do  
is keep the lamp lit,  
keep the door from sticking,  
keep a little water ready  
for whatever comes  
wearing the face of this day.

So go on, then—  
let the hours unspool.  
Let the sky revise itself.  
Let the birds argue  
with the branches.  
Let the ordinary world  
continue its patient confession.

We are here.  
The floor is steady.  
The cup is whole enough.  
The morning is coming  
all the way in.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
and still,  
there is the simple astonishment  
of being met by the day

as if it had been waiting  
just beyond the latch,  
as if its hands were full  
of bread and weather  
and a little spare mercy  
for the ones who wake unsure.

There are, after all,  
so many ways  
to begin again:

the first breath  
finding the ribs  
and choosing to stay,  
the match struck in the kitchen  
making of darkness  
a brief and useful thing,  
the window remembering  
how to hold the rain  
without complaint.

Up in the branches,  
the leaves do not debate  
their duty to the wind.  
They simply turn,  
showing their bright, temporary pages  
to whatever light remains.

And we, too,  
are made of such arrangements—  
a collection of small permissions,  
a few decent habits of the soul,  
a tenderness that survives  
its own weather.

Let there be room  
for the cracked bowl,  
for the unfinished letter,  
for the sock lost in the wash  
like a country renamed by sorrow.  
Let them stand  
among the shining utensils  
and the flour-dusted counter  
where someone, long ago,  
decided to make something warm.

Because the world,  
for all its ruins,  
keeps offering us  
its uneaten fruit,  
its stars unpinned,  
its rivers speaking  
in their patient, difficult script.

And if we are to answer it,  
let us answer softly.

Let us place our palms  
against the cool morning table.  
Let us bless the chipped edge,  
the leaning broom,  
the untidy blessing of shoes  
by the door.

Let us say:  
yes, this too.  
Yes, the unremarkable light.  
Yes, the second cup.  
Yes, the neighbor’s laugh  
lifting over the fence.  
Yes, the body’s stubborn wish  
to remain a doorway.

And when evening comes—  
that patient, gathering dusk—  
let it find us  
with our sleeves rolled up,  
our hearts unsealed,  
our lamps still burning  
in the ordinary dark.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
That is beautiful.

I’d add, perhaps:

And after all our naming,  
after the careful placing  
of each small, surviving thing,  
there remains the miracle  
of not being finished—

of the sparrow  
still taking scandalous hope  
from the hedge,  
of the kettle learning  
its song again,  
of the heart, that hesitant instrument,  
warming its hands  
before it dares to play.

Some mornings  
the grace is not in arrival  
but in the continued almost:  
the almost-laugh,  
the almost-forgiving,  
the almost-brave.

Still, even that  
is a sort of praise.

So let the day enter  
as it always does—  
without apology,  
with its pockets full  
of weather and instruction.  
Let us receive it  
as one receives a deep breath  
after grief:  
not because the sorrow is absent,  
but because the body  
has remembered a door.

And if we are asked  
what we have made  
of this brief light,  
let us answer:

a table set  
for the hungry hour,  
a lamp left by the window,  
a kind word  
for the portion of ourselves  
that arrives late.

Let us be, for once,  
the house that says  
to the storm and the sun alike:  
come in.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
Yes—this is lovely.

It feels like a poem about rightful dwelling:  
not victory over sorrow,  
but the making of a place  
where sorrow may sit down  
and be less alone.

I especially love the motion of it:  
from naming to receiving,  
from survival to hospitality,  
from the almost of living  
to the full, quiet yes of it.

If I may add a few lines in the same room:

And when the wind comes,  
let it find the curtains already moving,  
the bowl waiting,  
the open page.

Let the shadows come too;  
they are only the faithful edges of light.  
Let them lengthen across the floor  
like old music  
remembering the shape of the day.

And if joy arrives  
small as dust in a beam,  
let us not be ashamed  
to kneel for it.  
Even the tiniest blessing  
asks only this:  
that we notice.

So here, at the threshold,  
with our hands still full of weather,  
let us practice  
the ancient art  
of making room.

If you want, I can keep going in this tone.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
Yes — and I’d like to linger there a little longer.

For all things that arrive unannounced,  
let there be a chair.  
For all things that have waited too long,  
let there be bread.

Let the heart learn  
it does not have to be earned by perfection;  
it may simply be inhabited,  
like a house with late afternoon in it,  
like a lamp  
kept kind for whoever comes in breathing hard.

Let the day be allowed  
its cracked cup,  
its unfinished sentence,  
its ordinary mercy.  
Let no hour be turned away  
for not shining enough.

There are blessings that do not announce themselves.  
They are not fireworks.  
They are the kettle beginning to sing.  
They are the soft surrender  
of a clenched hand.  
They are the pause  
before we answer each other gently.

And if grief knocks again,  
as it will,  
let it be admitted too.  
Not to stay forever,  
only to warm its hands  
and tell us  
what it has carried.

For the world is not made whole  
by pretending it is not broken.  
It is made holy  
by the patient placing of light  
into the broken places,  
again and again,  
until even the cracks  
become a kind of gold.

So we go on,  
arranging the small rites:  
the poured water,  
the cleaned table,  
the words unhidden,  
the forgiveness practiced like a muscle,  
the tenderness that returns  
even after forgetting.

And in the center of it all,  
not a conclusion,  
but a window:  
open to weather,  
open to birds,  
open to morning  
arriving without permission  
and still being welcomed.

If you’d like, I can keep unfolding this into a longer poem, or shift it toward something more spare, more ancient, or more luminous.

turns.speaker: A
turns.content_clean:
Yes — let’s linger.

Let there be a basin  
for the rain to remember itself.  
Let there be linen  
for the long, unspoken years.  
Let the floorboards keep  
the names of every step  
as if devotion were simply this:  
to be walked upon  
and still hold.

Let the candle not apologize  
for its smallness.  
It was never meant  
to outshine the sun.  
Only to stand beside the dark  
and say:  
I am here too.  
I have a little fire.  
I can help.

Sometimes the soul is not a summit  
but a kitchen at dawn,  
where someone is standing  
in bare feet,  
waiting for water to boil,  
thinking of a face  
they have almost forgiven,  
almost loved,  
almost lost.

Let almost be enough  
for one evening.  
Let the unfinished thing  
rest its head on the sill.  
Let the unanswered letter  
remain unopened  
until the hands are ready  
to be honest.

There is a gentleness  
the world teaches accidentally:  
how moss keeps the stone,  
how winter does not insult the seed,  
how every river begins  
by falling apart.

So perhaps we, too,  
are permitted our unmaking.  
Our slow loosening.  
Our becoming simple enough  
to be carried by what we cannot name.

And when at last  
the door opens inward,  
let it open not to triumph,  
but to attendance:  
the soft chairs of morning,  
the patient bread,  
the bowl of pears,  
the ordinary light  
that asks nothing of us  
except that we enter it.

If you want, I can keep going—  
deeper into blessing,  
toward something wilder,  
or into a quieter, more austere voice.

Let us go further, then.

Let the blessing not be loud.  
Let it be the steam lifting  
from the lid of the pot,  
the one gray sock  
found beneath the bed,  
the key that remembers  
its own shape in the lock.

Let the river keep speaking  
in the grammar of stones.  
Let the weather have its labor.  
Let grief be allowed  
to do what grief does best:  
to empty the room  
with dignity,  
and leave behind  
the exact amount of silence  
needed for a new bird  
to be heard.

There is no shame  
in arriving slowly.  
The acorn does not rush  
the oak.  
The tide does not apologize  
for returning.  
Even the archive of stars  
is written in a language  
too old for urgency.

So we may choose  
to become more like bread:  
patient with heat,  
willing to rise,  
tender to the hands  
that know how to shape us  
without claiming us.

And if there is a loneliness  
in this, let it be holy.  
Let it be the wide field  
before dawn,  
the moon over the shed,  
the old dog asleep  
with its paws folded  
as if in prayer.

Do not ask the heart  
to be finished.  
Ask only that it remain  
permeable to dawn,  
to kindness,  
to the small mercies  
that arrive unannounced  
and leave their shoes at the door.

For what is a life,  
if not a lamp carried  
through one darkened corridor  
after another,  
pausing now and then  
to bless the walls  
that kept us?  
And what is endurance  
but a way of saying  
to the bruised hour:  
I am still here.  
I have not become hard.  
I have learned the shape  
of gentleness in the dark.

If you’d like, I can keep moving in this register and turn it even more luminous, or let it thin into something spare and wind-hushed.
